newsitem.title: UK: INTERVIEW-Rexam to go on chopping dead wood.
newsitem.headline: INTERVIEW-Rexam to go on chopping dead wood.

text.p: British-based industrial materials and packaging group Rexam Plc said on Tuesday it would continue apace with a disposals programme to get rid of underperforming businesses within its widely-spread structure.

Reforming chief executive Rolf Boerjesson, who heads a new management team that is reviewing all of Rexam's operations, said in an interview after announcing first-half results that the axe would fall in most parts of the company.
"We are looking at businesses with a weak position that are very much underperforming. They are spread over five out of seven of the (group's business) sectors," he told Reuters.
The disposal programme started earlier this year and built up during the spring, with units with annual sales equal to about 200 million stg sold already.

"There are businesses with sales of another 200 to 300 million stg that will be disposed over in the next 12 months," Boerjesson added, noting that these were already defined and there may be others if they cannot be made to perform better.

The aim of these moves, he explained, was to point Rexam's overall return on net assets back up towards 25 percent. During 1996 the return rate was just over 18 percent and in the seasonally weak first half the number came out at 17.1 percent.
Asked when he expected to be able to show a 25 percent return on assets, Boerjesson said, "I won't say when, but I'm not known to be patient."

Part of the uncertainty over future developments stems from a flat outlook in many markets because the prime mover of demand, industrial consumption, remains quite anaemic in Europe and the UK and is only partly offset by positive U.S. trends.
The chief executive said that packaging, where the company has a "mixed bag" of products, was an area of special concern at present as volumes in main markets were showing weakness.
Rexam's pretax profit in the first half fell to 83 million stg from 111 million stg in the year-ago period but Boerjesson said it was "obviously better" than the second half of 1995.

This had followed through to the extent that profits in July and August this year had been ahead of the corresponding period last year, but nevertheless, Boerjesson said "Our recommendation is to be rather cautious on the rest of the year."
The company maintained an unchanged ordinary dividend of 6.1 pence per share despite earnings per share dropping to 11.1 pence from 15.1 pence for the year-ago half.
